public_clues: The difference of two continuous real-valued functions on [0,1] is continuous on [0,1].
A continuous real-valued function on [0,1] that is never zero cannot take both positive and negative values.
original_question: For every pair of continuous functions $f,g:[0,1] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that \(\max\{f(x):x \in [0,1]\} = \max\{g(x):x \in [0,1]\}\), is there always a point $c \in [0,1]$ such that $f(c) = g(c)$? Answer yes or no.
alternative_question: For every pair of continuous real functions f,g on[0,1] with equal definite integrals over[0,1], must there be c in[0,1] with f(c)=g(c)?
proof: h=f-g is continuous. If h never vanishes, the intermediate value theorem makes it strictly positive everywhere or strictly negative everywhere. Compactness gives a strictly positive minimum for h or -h, hence the integral of h is nonzero, contradicting the equal-integral premise.
clue_grounding: The difference f-g is continuous in both problems.
Assuming no equality point makes f-g nonzero; the sign lemma applies in both proofs.
